Context/Background:
Cancer-induced systemic inflammation is a dominant feature of cancer progression and metastatic spread. Clinically, systemic accumulation of myeloid cells is strongly correlated to poor prognosis in multiple solid malignancies, including breast cancer and a high neutrophil-to-lymphocyte (NLR) ratio is consistently associated with adverse outcomes. We, and others, previously published that primary tumors induce systemic accumulation and activation of neutrophils leading to enhanced metastatic spread in preclinical mouse models. In steady state, hematopoietic stem cells (HSCs) give rise to all circulating blood cells through a series of progressively restrictive differentiation steps regulated by coordinated and temporal expression of transcription factors (TFs), leading to balanced bone marrow (BM) output. However, the molecular processes driving chronic, cancer-induced hematopoiesis, which leads to systemic inflammation, remain poorly understood.

We have previously demonstrated that expansion of metastasis-supporting neutrophils in mammary tumor-bearing K14cre;Cdh1fl/fl;Trp53fl/fl (KEP) mice is driven by an inflammatory cascade in which tumor associated macrophage (TAM)-derived IL-1β leads to elevated serum levels of G-CSF, the principal instructor of neutrophil generation. To understand how and at what stage of differentiation tumors drive neutrophil expansion, we clustered the genes upregulated in tumor-bearing mice based on their dynamics along the neutrophil pseudotime trajectory. We identified three groups of differentially expressed genes in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs) from KEP mice, which we termed early, middle, and late, based on their expression patterns. 

Early genes showed significant enrichment of an HSC-specific gene set. Upregulated early genes were overexpressed in HSCs and multipotent progenitors (MPPs) from KEP mice compared to cells from control mice but were repressed in cells that were further along the inferred neutrophil differentiation trajectory. Middle genes were defined as genes that were expressed around the transition from MPP to granulocyte monocyte progenitor (GMP). Lastly, upregulated/downregulated late genes, expressed in late GMP, granulocyte progenitor (GP), and pro-neutrophil (ProNeu) populations, were found to be expressed prematurely and at a higher level in progenitors from KEP mice.
Prompt: Provide a summary of the relevant pathways and genes that are up and down regulated in KEP vs WT mice in early, intermediate and late neutrophil development, focusing on how and at what stage of differentiation tumors drive neutrophil expansion.

Introduction/Context  
KEP mice (K14^cre;Cdh1^fl/fl;Trp53^fl/fl) develop mammary tumors that drive systemic neutrophil expansion via TAM-derived IL-1β and elevated G-CSF. Here, HSPCs from KEP versus WT bone marrow were profiled along a neutrophil pseudotime trajectory and DE genes were clustered into Early, Intermediate, and Late groups according to where they peak during neutrophil differentiation. The provided dataset (Garner_2025_Cancer_Cell_TableS1-ClusterMembership.csv) lists 1,142 genes labeled “Up” or “Down” in Early, Intermediate, or Late clusters (no replicates or effect sizes specified). ORA on each gene list (MSigDB Hallmark 2020 and KEGG 2021 Human) reveals stage-specific pathway enrichments.  

Keywords  
• neutrophil differentiation • JAK-STAT signaling • inflammatory response • metabolic reprogramming • unfolded protein response  

Candidate Genes  
CEBPA, SPI1, IL1R1, STAT3, MPO, CSF3R

Analysis  
Early‐stage upregulated genes in KEP HSPCs are dominated by inflammatory and JAK-STAT modules (e.g., IFN responses, IL-6/JAK/STAT3, IL-2/STAT5), consistent with tumor-driven cytokine signaling. Intermediate clusters shift toward metabolic-reprogramming and proliferation programs (Myc targets, mTORC1, amino-acid metabolism, G2-M checkpoint), indicating enhanced biosynthetic and cell-cycle activity. Late cluster enrichment of UPR, sustained mTORC1/Myc/E2F activity, and p53 signaling suggests chronic ER stress and proliferative exhaustion in maturing neutrophil progenitors. Downregulated early pathways include negative regulation of cell-growth signals (Notch, UV response, IFN) whereas late downregulation hits key differentiation regulators (p53, Wnt/β-catenin, G2-M). Overall, tumors skew neutrophil output by ramping inflammatory JAK-STAT cues at the HSC/MPP stage, fueling metabolic and proliferative drive mid‐differentiation, and inducing stress pathways prematurely in late progenitors.

Comparisons  
Early inflammatory cues (JAK/STAT) are KEP-specific and absent in WT, whereas intermediate metabolic programs (Myc/mTORC1) emerge predominantly in KEP. Late clusters in KEP show heightened proteostatic stress (UPR) not seen in WT. Downregulated modules overlap less across stages, indicating stage-specific suppression of differentiation checkpoints.  

Implications  
Tumor-derived IL-1β/G-CSF may rewire HSCs via STAT3/STAT5 to favor neutrophil output, then co-opt metabolic and UPR pathways mid-differentiation, potentially yielding hyperactivated, metastasis-supporting neutrophils. Targeting JAK/STAT signaling or metabolic checkpoints (e.g., mTORC1, Myc) may restore balanced hematopoiesis and limit neutrophil-mediated metastasis.  

Next Steps & Clarification  
1. Validate STAT3 phosphorylation and IL1R1 induction at the HSC/MPP stage by flow cytometry.  
2. Profile metabolic flux (e.g., serine/glycine) in GMPs from KEP versus WT to confirm intermediate-stage reprogramming.  
3. Test UPR inhibitor impact on late-stage progenitor survival and neutrophil function in KEP BM.  
4. Assess expression of G-CSF receptor (CSF3R) and PU.1 (SPI1) across clusters to link systemic cytokines to transcriptional reprogramming.
